reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / standard metabolic references
clinicalPearls: The most common lysosomal storage disorder, caused by deficient activity of the enzyme glucocerebrosidase (acid beta-glucosidase) and inherited in an autosomal recessive manner
Undegraded glucocerebroside accumulates within macrophages, producing the characteristic lipid-laden 'Gaucher cells' seen in marrow and other tissues
Type 1 is non-neuronopathic and dominates in adults and older children, with hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenias, and bone involvement but sparing of the central nervous system
Type 2 is the acute neuronopathic form of infancy with rapid neurological deterioration and a poor outlook, while type 3 shows slower, chronic neurological disease
Bone manifestations include marrow infiltration, painful crises, avascular necrosis, and the classic Erlenmeyer-flask deformity of the distal femur
Splenomegaly with thrombocytopenia and anaemia is a frequent presenting picture and can mimic a haematological malignancy
Enzyme replacement therapy is effective for the visceral and haematological features of type 1, and oral substrate reduction therapy is an alternative in selected patients
Disease-modifying therapy does not correct neurological disease because infused enzyme does not cross the blood-brain barrier
Increased susceptibility to Parkinsonism is recognised in patients and carriers with glucocerebrosidase gene variants
reference.pathophysiology: Gaucher disease results from biallelic pathogenic variants in the GBA gene encoding lysosomal glucocerebrosidase (acid beta-glucosidase). Reduced enzyme activity impairs breakdown of glucocerebroside (glucosylceramide), which accumulates predominantly within the lysosomes of macrophages of the reticuloendothelial system. These engorged macrophages (Gaucher cells) infiltrate the spleen, liver, bone marrow, and, in neuronopathic forms, the nervous system, driving organomegaly, marrow replacement with cytopenias, and skeletal disease. The pattern and severity of residual enzyme activity, influenced by genotype, largely determine whether the phenotype is non-neuronopathic (type 1) or neuronopathic (types 2 and 3).
additionalDifferentials: Other lysosomal storage disorders with hepatosplenomegaly
Haematological malignancy such as leukaemia or lymphoma
Myelofibrosis or other causes of splenomegaly with cytopenia
Chronic liver disease with portal hypertension
additionalInvestigations: Assay of glucocerebrosidase enzyme activity in leukocytes or cultured fibroblasts
GBA molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis and guide counselling
Full blood count to detect anaemia and thrombocytopenia
Plasma biomarkers such as chitotriosidase or glucosylsphingosine (lyso-Gb1) to support diagnosis and monitor disease
Skeletal imaging including MRI to assess marrow infiltration and bone complications
redFlags: Rapid neurological regression in infancy suggesting acute neuronopathic (type 2) disease
Severe thrombocytopenia with bleeding or profound anaemia
Acute bone pain crisis or evidence of avascular necrosis
Massive splenomegaly with risk of rupture or hypersplenism
reference.prognosis: Type 1 disease generally has a good outlook, especially with enzyme replacement or substrate reduction therapy, which reverses much of the visceral and haematological burden. Type 2 carries a poor prognosis with early death, whereas type 3 has an intermediate course with progressive neurological involvement despite treatment of systemic features.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing splenomegaly with cytopenia as a primary haematological malignancy and pursuing unnecessary invasive workup
Assuming enzyme replacement therapy will halt neurological progression in neuronopathic forms
Overlooking bone disease, which can progress even when visceral parameters improve
Failing to offer genetic counselling and carrier testing to at-risk relatives
